title: Anansi and His Six Sons
text:
In an Ashanti tale, Anansi the spider had six sons, and each had one special gift. One could see trouble far away. One could build roads. One could drink up a river. One could skin game. One could throw stones with perfect aim. And one could act as a cushion and catch whatever fell.

One day Anansi went on a long journey and fell into a river, where a great fish swallowed him. Far away at home, the son who saw trouble knew at once that their father was in danger. The road builder made a road to the river. The river drinker drank the water until the fish lay exposed. The skinner cut the fish open, and Anansi climbed out.

But at that moment a falcon swooped down, seized Anansi and flew off with him. The stone thrower hit the falcon with a single stone, and Anansi fell from the sky. The son who was a cushion ran beneath him and caught him safely.

Later Anansi found a beautiful globe of light in the forest and wanted to give it to the son who had saved him. But all six had done it together, and they argued over who deserved it. Finally the sky god Nyame took the light up into the sky, where it still hangs as the moon.
lesson: A rescue or a project often depends on a chain of different skills, and every link matters. When the whole team made the result, arguing over one winner can lose the prize.
people: Anansi and his six sons, the sky god Nyame
source: Harold Courlander and Albert Kofi Prempeh, The Hat-Shaking Dance and Other Ashanti Tales from Ghana (1957), Anansi's Rescue from the River
caveat: The tale is best known from 20th century retellings, and the sons' gifts and names vary between versions.
